newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia minister dismayed at threats to foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Russia minister dismayed at threats to foreigners.

text.p: Russia's interior minister expressed his dismay on Friday after two British businessmen and their families were evacuated from Moscow because they had received threats.
An official from U.S. tobacco group Philip Morris Companies Inc said two of its Moscow-based staff had left with their families on Wednesday night.

"We can confirm that two employees and their families were flown out of Russia as a precautionary measure after a threat was received," said Andrew White, director of corporate affairs in Moscow. He declined to give details of the threat.
"We have notified the authorities and they're taking appropriate action to resolve this issue," he said.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said the incident was a blow to Russian reforms which depended on foreign investment. He did not specify whether the threat was extortion or from business rivals but said police would try to catch the culprits.
"This does not, of course, help to improve the investment climate in the country," Kulikov told a news conference.
"We understand this very well and we are always very upset when we have to consider such cases," he added.
"We always try to take measures and find those guilty and protect foreign investors' interests because our budget cannot provide enough money to invest in the economy."
Although threats and murders against Russian businessmen have become commonplace in the wild atmosphere of post-Soviet capitalism in Russia, incidents against Western businessmen are relatively rare.

But in November last year American Paul Tatum, part-owner of one of the city's most prominent hotels, was shot dead near the building's entrance. An American reporter investigating the case also left the country within hours after he was threatened.
Neither the Tatum case nor many of the frequent assassinations of Russian businessmen through bomb blasts or shootings have been solved.
Kulikov said much had been done to make it safer to do business in Russia but that an end to Wild West-type behaviour would not come until the economy began to grow.
"Until the real sector gives results, it will be difficult to hope for normal life and prosperity in the country from the economic point of view," he said.
White said the evacuation on Wednesday was the first of its kind by Philip Morris, which has invested in cigarette factories across the former Soviet Union.
About two thirds of Russia's men and a third of its women smoke, making the country an important market for the company.
But Philip Morris' successful marketing techniques have made it enemies. In 1992 a series of bomb blasts damaged kiosks in St Petersburg selling the company's Marlboro cigarettes at low prices.
